The only criticisms that I really have from seeing the footage is that the level design is somewhat counter-intuitive (seriously, who would design those house layouts in real life like that?), often leading to being trapped in corridors by several "human shields" (Police officers), and that the AI itself is somewhat clunky, and could deal with a little polish. Personally I don't think I will buy it - not out of principal or "MUH TRIGGURS", but that it just doesn't hold my interest beyond the destructibility of the world.

First, disclaimer, I would really like to say that Arch has little to no place in a server environment. If you want to run a Linux based server, I would suggest you try Debian, Fedora/RedHat, or OpenSuse. That being said, there are some reasons why you may need something like Arch on a server. Outlines below are some reasons.

  1. If you need something lightweight, or your hardware is a limitation

Sure, Debian netinst and others are very light weight, but you really just cant compare to how minimal an Arch Linux installation is. You can have a pretty happy server with less than 30 packages, while Debian 8.0 Jessie netinst comes with 70+ on a GUIless installation.

  1. If the security of your packages is a huge concern.

Sure, rolling packages can break things, open more security wholes, and cause havoc, but more often than not, you get new patches, fixes, and features months before everyone else.

  1. If you need a larger base of software.

Although filling your server up with packages may not be a great idea, having a larger repository through the AUR becaomes immensly helpful when you want to install experemental software, or smaller projects to make managing and using your server easier.

  1. When you want access to a massive Wiki and forums to help you through any problem that may arise.

There is no denying that the Arch Wiki is one of the most powerful GNU/Linux recources out there, with documentation on pretty much every package, feature, tool, and command out there on the net. Also, the arch forums is a really strong community that is around to help you with just about every issue you may encounter.

BUT, as anyone who has used or even heard of Arch knows that just one simple pacman -Syu can put your system out of commision for a few hours while you backdate packages and scour the forums for an obscure issue that came out of nowhere.

Luckily, there are a few ways to make Arch Linux more fit to a stable server environment.

-improvement #1

Install the linux-lts package

The linux-lts package is an alternative Arch kernel package based upon Linux kernel 3.14 and is available in the core repository. This particular kernel version enjoys long-term support (LTS) from upstream, including security fixes and some feature backports.

Pretty much all you have to do is

sudo pacman -Sy linux-lts

And then automatically update your grub by running

grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg

after rebooting, type uname -a to make sure you are on kernel 3.14

-improvement #2

Keep old versions of packages in your /var/ partition, so if an update does break something, you can easily backdate a package.

-improvement #3

Keep track of the packages you install, and remove orphaned dependancies. This can save you from a lot of issues in the future

Thats really all I have for today, but if you have any more suggestions, I would love ot hear them!
